tagline: White quartz dunes and river country carry a fur post’s name
intro: Fort Henry Historic Byway is a two-lane eastern Idaho drive with no mountain passes, linking white quartz dunes and Henrys Fork country. Visit Idaho highlights the scenic byway’s dunes, fishing and Indigenous history, and lists 90.4 miles with a driving time of two hours and 30 minutes. The Henrys Fork meanders through a high-desert floodplain, while wind has built the St. Anthony dunes to heights of 400 feet.

The byway takes its name from Fort Henry, the early settlement built by Andrew Henry near present-day St. Anthony. Henry entered the Snake River plateau in 1810 while working for the Missouri Fur Company. His post was short-lived, but his name also remains on the river that passes through St. Anthony. Rail travel later shaped Ashton, where the town’s founding and first scheduled train service both came in 1906. The Yellowstone Branch carried passengers toward Yellowstone and made Ashton a winter terminus.

From the North Rexburg US 20 exit, Salem Highway leads toward the St. Anthony Sand Dunes on Red Road. A-2 continues north, then east to Island Park and US 20. The other leg starts at Salem Highway and 500 North, heads east to St. Anthony, then follows old US 191 past Chester to Ashton.

moments.title: St. Anthony Sand Dunes
moments.text: White quartz sand covers 10,600 acres north and northwest of St. Anthony, with dunes reaching 400 feet high. Wind has piled that sand into the dunes that give this stop its shape. Visit Idaho presents the dunes as a place for hiking and ATV riding. The same area has a seasonal wildlife role: 2,500 elk winter near the dunes, alongside mule deer and moose. These animals shed antlers during their time here, and collectors come in spring. A wilderness study area protects white-sand country here, alongside the dunes’ documented uses for recreation and winter habitat.
moments.notice: Notice the white quartz sand that forms the dunes.

moments.title: Camas Meadows Battleground
moments.text: Camas Meadows Battle Sites is a National Historic Landmark near Kilgore. Kilgore sits beside East Camas Creek, and Visit Idaho includes the battle sites among the byway’s nearby historic places.

moments.title: Ashton
moments.text: Ashton’s rail connection began with its founding in 1906, when the first scheduled trains arrived. Ashton became a winter rail terminus because the Yellowstone Branch north of town was left unplowed until spring. Dog teams supplied winter transportation to the snowbound country beyond it. In March 1917, the first American Dog Derby ran 55 miles down that unplowed branch from West Yellowstone to Ashton. A blizzard delayed the finish by two days. The next race used a figure-eight course through Ashton, bringing teams through town twice per lap; Union Pacific later brought spectators on special trains.
